findings.note: A mutated test run that is KILLED rather than exited is scored as a proven kill. exec() (verify.go:183-186) returns ProcessState.ExitCode() and a nil error whenever the process was waited on, and a signal-killed process yields ExitCode() == -1 with err discarded (confirmed empirically: exec.CommandContext + CombinedOutput on a deadline-killed command returns 'signal: killed', ProcessState non-nil, ExitCode -1). Step 4 (verify.go:144-152) then sees err==nil and code!=0 and returns PinResult{Proven:true, Outcome:PinProven} with Detail claiming '... fails the tests and the restored code passes them'. Two concrete paths: (a) the mutation introduces a non-terminating loop (a classic mutation-testing timeout mutant) or merely pushes the suite past the deadline - the caller at internal/fsm/cli/wiring.go:391 sets no Timeout, so defaultVerifyTimeout of 10 minutes applies - and the fix agent's claim is recorded as PROVEN although no test ever failed; (b) the operator interrupts the run (cmd/metareview/main.go:106 passes context.Background(), so Ctrl-C/parent cancellation is the only bound) while a step-4 run is in flight, and that pin comes back Proven. PinUnverifiable, the outcome invented for exactly 'the tree could not answer', is unreachable for the killed case because err is nil. This defeats the single property the package exists to establish; the fix is to return the error (or a distinct killed signal) when ProcessState.Exited() is false, and treat it as PinUnverifiable.

findings.note: status.BuildFor reports blocked:false for a target that has never been reviewed, so the Stop hook this same PR ships passes for any work that was never gated - which is the exact failure the hook was written to prevent. BuildFor (status.go:65-105) matches s.Target == target by byte-exact string equality, sets MustClear from the survivors and Blocked = len(MustClear) > 0; a target that matches nothing is indistinguishable in the JSON from a target that was reviewed and came back clean. Real Target values in this repository are strings like `current branch` (docs/metareview/reviews/*-pr-ready-*.md:5) and `docs/specs/....md`, so any METAREVIEW_TARGET an operator sets that is not one of those - e.g. the path of the file the agent just edited - makes `metareview status --json --target ...` emit must_clear:[] and exit 0, and hooks/pre-finish.sh exits 0 on that. An agent that never runs a metareview gate at all therefore satisfies the Stop hook trivially. The hook's own doc states 'a check that did not run must not read as a check that passed'; this is that case. The report needs a way to say 'no review matched this target' (a matched/reviewed count, or a distinct exit code) so the hook can block or warn instead of waving through. Note the unscoped default is still fail-closed, which bounds the impact to operators who set METAREVIEW_TARGET.

findings.note: The fingerprint dedup drops genuinely distinct surviving mutants. MutationContext.Findings (internal/reviewers/mutation.go:34-40) keys `seen` on f.Fingerprint, and the survivor fingerprint is 'mutation:survived:<Operator>:<File>:<Line>' (internal/mutation/report.go:126) - Mutant.Column is parsed and stored by BOTH engines (internal/mutation/stryker.go:52, internal/mutation/gremlins.go:42) but is not in the fingerprint. Because `seen` is declared outside the per-report loop it also collapses within one report. Concretely, `return a < 10 && b < 20` on one line yields two CONDITIONALS_BOUNDARY mutants at the same file:line with different columns; if both survive, exactly one becomes a finding and the gate under-reports the work. The dangerous interaction is with overrides: per CLAUDE.md an `overridden` record suppresses rediscovery of the same fingerprint, so a human who reviews and grants an override for one survivor at that line silently silences a second, never-reviewed survivor at the same line and operator. Separately, the doc comment's stated purpose - 'running two engines over the same package must not double-report the site they agree on' - is not achieved, because gremlins operator names come from `type` (CONDITIONALS_BOUNDARY-style) and stryker's from `mutatorName` (ConditionalExpression-style), so cross-engine fingerprints for the same site never collide. Include Column in the survivor fingerprint, and either normalise operator vocabularies or drop the cross-engine claim from the comment.

findings.note: Verify has no aggregate bound and re-does the expensive setup per pin. verifyOne copies the entire tree (verify.go:102-109, whole-file reads into memory, excluding only .git and node_modules) and re-runs the full baseline suite (verify.go:124) for every pin, so N pins cost N tree copies and up to 3N full test-suite runs. Timeout is per command, not per Verify, and the caller sets none (internal/fsm/cli/wiring.go:391) while cmd/metareview/main.go:106 passes context.Background(), so nothing bounds the whole node. The pin count is chosen by the fix agent - the untrusted party this node exists to check - so 20 pins is a legitimately reachable multi-hour hang. This compounds finding 1, because the operator's natural response to the hang (Ctrl-C) is the cancellation path that produces a false Proven. Copying and baselining once per Verify, and giving Verify an overall deadline, would fix both the cost and the blast radius.
